summary: Uprising keeps the core deck-building/worker-placement loop of Dune: Imperium intact while adding new factions, sandworm-riding, spy tokens, and asymmetric team play for six; it plays fast and tense, with agonizing worker-placement choices every round. It feels both familiar to fans of the original and meaningfully fresh thanks to new cards, the Fremen/Smugglers factions, and the redesigned Landsraad-style contract system.
praised: Tense worker placement with meaningful blocking and denial
Strong theme integration (spice, sandworms, factions, conflict)
High replayability from combat/conflict variability and modular content
New 6-player team mode adds a fresh way to experience the game
Streamlines and improves on some base-game rough edges (contracts, tech cards)
criticised: Can feel like 'more of the same' to owners of the original Dune: Imperium
Rules overhead increases with new mechanisms (sandworms, spies, contracts)
Compatibility/integration with base game and expansions can be confusing to track
Combat can occasionally feel swingy or luck-influenced via troop/agent card draws

interaction.kind: worker placement blocking, area control combat, and open drafting

scoring.why: Victory points come from combat wins, Landsraad/contract objectives, Fremen alliance and sandworm actions, and intrigue/tech card synergies, so multiple viable scoring paths compete for the win.
